blocks.text: Cyclic sort is one instance of a broader idea worth naming: when values are bounded by the array's own length, the **array can index itself**.
The array as its own hash map

A hash map normally answers "have I seen value x?" in O(1), at a cost of O(N) space. But if every value is a valid index, you can store that information **inside the array itself** — no extra structure.

items: **Swap into place** — cyclic sort. Position encodes presence.
**Mark by negation** — flip the sign at index `|v|` to record that `v` was seen.
**Mark by offset** — add N to the element at the target index; the original survives as the remainder.

blocks.text: The most common variant. For values in 1..N, visiting value `v` flips the sign of the element at index `v - 1`. A negative entry later means that index was visited.
`Math.abs` is essential — by the time you read a value it may already have been negated by an earlier step, and the magnitude is what carries the real number.

These tricks **mutate the input**. That is fine when the problem permits it and a serious bug when it does not. If the caller needs the original, either restore it in a second pass or use the honest O(N) map.
Interview problems that specify O(1) space are usually inviting exactly this trick. Production code rarely wants it — a hash set is clearer, and clarity is normally worth more than N words of memory.
Information does not require its own storage if it can be encoded in something you already hold. Here the encodings are position and sign — a bit of state hiding in plain sight.
